ideas.title: World models are bifurcating into "state-executing" and "pixel-generating" paradigms — the gap is a hybrid that does both for interactive reasoning.
ideas.body: State World Models explicitly separate rule execution from pixel generation, arguing that action-conditioned video alone can't model navigation and interaction [State World Models]. Meanwhile, AnyGoal shows world models trained only on expert rollouts fail to generalize to novel goals [AnyGoal]. The unexplored direction is whether a state-space core (symbolic or latent) can drive a generative pixel decoder for *counterfactual* simulation — letting agents "imagine" interventions that were never in the training distribution. This would require disentangling dynamics from rendering, which neither current approach does cleanly.
ideas.signal: State World Models, AnyGoal, InfiniDream

ideas.title: Physical RSI scaling laws are being measured, but nobody has asked what the *policy representation* itself must look like to sustain recursive improvement.
ideas.body: The observational scaling law work on LLM-as-policy quantifies where physical RSI capability comes from [Where is Physical RSI capability from?]. The gap is architectural: if RSI emerges from scaling, does it require a specific policy encoding (e.g., latent actions vs. token outputs), or is it purely a function of model size and environment richness? The paper's framing suggests capability is an emergent property, but no one has tested whether RSI saturates when the policy's action space is constrained. A controlled ablation across action representations would be immediately publishable and strategically important.
ideas.signal: Where is Physical RSI capability from?, HarnessPro

ideas.title: Multimodal memory for visual agents is being treated as a retrieval problem, not a *consolidation* problem.
ideas.body: OpenVLHarness introduces multimodal memory for real-world visual tool use [OpenVLHarness], and MemT-1.0 pushes toward "memory-native evolution" [MemT-1.0]. But both treat memory as an external store queried on demand. The gap is *when and how* memories get consolidated into the model's weights versus kept in context — the biological analogue of hippocampal replay. No current system has a principled schedule for converting frequently-used multimodal memories into parameter updates, which would dramatically reduce inference-time context cost.
ideas.signal: OpenVLHarness, MemT-1.0, Kronecker Delta Rule

ideas.title: Text-to-image without language pretraining opens a path to *non-linguistic* conditional generation — but nobody has tested it on non-human "prompts."
ideas.body: The finding that strong T2I is possible without language pretraining [Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining] implies the text encoder is not doing semantic heavy lifting. The unexplored consequence: if language is just a convenient conditioning signal, then *any* structured signal (neural activity, sketches, haptic patterns, musical scores) could serve as the conditioning modality with the same architecture. This is a research gap with immediate applications in accessibility and brain-computer interfaces, especially given concurrent work on scaling PEFT for brain encoding [Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding].
ideas.signal: Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining, Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding

ideas.title: Egocentric world models are being built from human experience, but the *temporal granularity* of that experience is unexamined.
ideas.body: EgoXperience and Holi-World both learn world-grounded representations from human egocentric video [EgoXperience, Holi-World]. The gap: these models treat all moments as equally informative, but human experience is highly non-uniform in its learning value — moments of surprise, error, or deliberate practice carry disproportionate weight. No one has tested whether filtering egocentric data by *learning signal density* (e.g., prediction error magnitude) produces better world models with far less data. This connects directly to the RSI scaling question: what makes some experience more "improving" than others?
ideas.signal: EgoXperience, Holi-World, Ropedia W0

ideas.title: Hybrid architectures show "competing learning" dynamics — but the competition itself could be a training signal.
ideas.body: Competing Learning in Hybrid Architectures reveals that recurrence and softmax attention compete during training [Competing Learning in Hybrid Architectures]. The gap is treating this competition as a *feature* rather than a bug: if different architectural components specialize on different input regimes (e.g., recurrence for local structure, attention for long-range dependencies), then the *routing decision* becomes a learnable meta-signal. No current work frames hybrid training as an explicit specialization game with a router.
ideas.signal: Competing Learning in Hybrid Architectures, Kronecker Delta Rule

ideas.title: Agent world models are being synthesized for computer use, but the synthesis process itself is not self-improving.
ideas.body: Agent World Model in the Wild focuses on synthesizing environments for computer-use agents [Agent World Model in the Wild]. The gap: the environment generator is static. If the generator were trained adversarially against the agent — producing environments that exploit the agent's current weaknesses — you'd have a curriculum that automatically scales with agent capability. This is the missing link between world-model synthesis and RSI.
ideas.signal: Agent World Model in the Wild, HarnessPro, AnyGoal

ideas.title: Context compression is being evaluated for faithfulness, but not for *reversibility* — can the original be reconstructed well enough to answer unseen questions?
ideas.body: KEEP-Bench evaluates evidence preservation in context compression [KEEP-Bench], and LatComm explores latent communication between LLMs [LatComm]. The gap: current metrics ask "does the compressed context preserve the answer to known questions?" but not "can the compressed context support *novel* queries that weren't anticipated at compression time?" This is the difference between summarization and true lossless compression. A benchmark for *query-agnostic* reversibility would expose whether current methods are actually compressing or just selectively discarding.
ideas.signal: KEEP-Bench, LatComm, Same Simulation Different Evidence

ideas.title: Safety is being "mid-trained" into models, but the interaction between safety mid-training and later capability fine-tuning is uncharted.
ideas.body: Safety Mid-Training proposes internalizing safety as a foundational capability [Safety Mid-Training]. The gap: what happens when a safety-mid-trained model is subsequently fine-tuned for a specific capability? Does the safety "stick" or get overwritten? The catastrophic forgetting literature suggests it might not survive, but no one has tested this systematically. This is a critical safety question with immediate policy implications.
ideas.signal: Safety Mid-Training, Competing Learning in Hybrid Architectures

ideas.title: Brain encoding models are scaling with PEFT, but the *direction* of transfer — from brain to model — is unexplored.
ideas.body: Scaling PEFT for brain encoding shows that parameter-efficient fine-tuning can scale to neural data [Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding]. The gap: this work goes from stimuli → brain activity. The reverse direction — using brain activity to *steer* or *condition* generative models — is wide open, especially given the finding that language pretraining isn't necessary for T2I. A brain-to-image system built on the no-language-pretraining architecture would be a landmark result.
ideas.signal: Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding, Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining

ideas.title: "Faithful adaptation" tooling for manga, comics, and storyboards — the first AI product that respects source material.
ideas.body: Manga2Animate demonstrates an agentic framework for faithful manga-to-animation with script and storyboard planning [Manga2Animate]. The product gap: creators don't want *generic* animation — they want adaptation that preserves panel composition, dialogue, and artistic intent. A tool that ingests manga/comics and produces *storyboard-accurate* animatics with editable script and camera planning would be immediately valuable to studios and independent creators. The technical moat is the faithfulness constraint, not the generation quality.
ideas.signal: Manga2Animate, Mise-en-Video

ideas.title: A "world model gym" for embodied AI — stress-testing robots and agents against adversarially generated environments.
ideas.body: Laplace Intelligence is already red-teaming robots and self-driving cars with AI agents and simulation [TechCrunch AI]. But the academic work on world model generalization [AnyGoal] and agent environment synthesis [Agent World Model in the Wild] suggests a more ambitious product: a continuous environment-generation service that automatically produces scenarios an agent fails on, then re-trains against them. This is "RSI as a service" for embodied AI companies.
ideas.signal: AnyGoal, Agent World Model in the Wild, Laplace Intelligence

ideas.title: A "memory-native" personal AI that consolidates your multimodal history into its weights, not just its context window.
ideas.body: MemT-1.0's memory-native evolution [MemT-1.0] and OpenVLHarness's multimodal memory [OpenVLHarness] point to a product that doesn't just *retrieve* your past but *internalizes* it. Imagine a personal assistant that gets better at *your* specific visual environment, tools, and workflows over time — not by holding everything in a giant context, but by periodically fine-tuning small adapters on your consolidated experience. The technical challenge is the consolidation schedule; the product moat is that it genuinely improves with use.
ideas.signal: MemT-1.0, OpenVLHarness, Kronecker Delta Rule

ideas.title: A "decompilation as a service" platform for legacy software preservation and modernization.
ideas.body: The AI mass decompilation trend [Simon Willison] is currently a hobbyist phenomenon. But the product opportunity is systematic: enterprises with legacy binaries (banking, industrial control, medical devices) need source code recovery for security audits, compliance, and modernization. A platform that combines AI decompilation with *verification* (does the recovered source recompile to equivalent behavior?) would be far more valuable than the current ad-hoc tools.
ideas.signal: Simon Willison on AI decompilation, OpenCode hack

ideas.title: An "agent firewall" for enterprises that treats AI agents as insider threats — with behavioral baselining.
ideas.body: Microsoft is already telling enterprises to watch agents like insider threats [TechCrunch AI], and hackers are using agent armies to breach sites [The Verge AI]. The product gap: current security tools don't understand *agent behavior* — they see API calls, not intent. A firewall that baselines normal agent behavior and flags anomalous patterns (unusual tool combinations, unexpected data exfiltration, deviation from declared goals) would be a new security category.
ideas.signal: Microsoft on AI agents as insider threats, The Verge on AI agent hacker, Google DeepMind on securing AI agents

ideas.title: A "faithful evidence" layer for LLM agents — ensuring tool outputs are actually read, not just filed away.
ideas.body: Same Simulation, Different Evidence shows that agents lose accuracy when tool outputs are saved to files instead of kept in context [Same Simulation, Different Evidence]. The product: an agent middleware that *verifies* the agent actually processed the evidence — by checking intermediate reasoning, generating follow-up queries, or using a separate verifier model. This is a trust layer for agentic workflows in high-stakes domains.
ideas.signal: Same Simulation Different Evidence, KEEP-Bench, HarnessPro

ideas.title: A "plant translator" that goes beyond novelty — using electrical signals for precision agriculture.
ideas.body: Electric Plant's AI translator for plant electricity [TechCrunch AI] is a curiosity today. The product opportunity is *not* "talk to your plants" but *precision stress detection*: identifying water stress, nutrient deficiency, or pest pressure days before visible symptoms, using cheap electrical sensors. This is a B2B agricultural SaaS play, not a consumer gadget.
ideas.signal: TechCrunch on Electric Plant

ideas.title: A "scam warfare" platform that deploys LLM agents to waste scammers' time at scale.
ideas.body: Game of Phones uses game theory and LLMs in "Bot Wars" to counteract phone scams [Game of Phones]. The product: a telecom-integrated service that automatically detects scam calls and deploys engaging AI decoys to tie up scammers, while collecting intelligence on their tactics. The value is both defensive (protecting victims) and offensive (making scams economically unviable).
ideas.signal: Game of Phones, Google DeepMind on scam detection

ideas.title: A "benchmark science" platform that treats evaluation as a continuous, adversarial process — not a static test.
ideas.body: Moritz Hardt's call for AI benchmarking as a science [Quanta Magazine] and the VPD evaluation adversary finding systematic defects [LessWrong] point to a product: a continuous evaluation platform that actively *searches* for model weaknesses, updates benchmarks when they saturate, and provides *causal* explanations for failures. This is "evals as a living system," not a one-time certification.
ideas.signal: Quanta on Hardt, LessWrong on VPD, GenOlympiad

ideas.title: Prediction: Within 18 months, a major lab will release a text-to-image model with *no text encoder at all* — and it will match or beat language-pretrained models on standard benchmarks.
ideas.body: The finding that language pretraining isn't necessary for strong T2I [Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining] is currently academic. The contrarian bet is that this becomes the *default* architecture because it's simpler, cheaper, and more flexible. Falsifiable: if no major lab adopts this by mid-2028, the bet fails.
ideas.signal: Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining

ideas.title: Prediction: "Memory-native" models will be the next architecture war, replacing the context-window arms race — and the winner will be judged on *consolidation efficiency*, not retrieval accuracy.
ideas.body: MemT-1.0 [MemT-1.0] and the Kronecker Delta Rule for long-context linear attention [Kronecker Delta Rule] both point toward memory as a first-class architectural primitive. The contrarian bet: context length stops being the headline metric, replaced by "how much can the model *internalize* per parameter." Falsifiable: if the next generation of frontier models still advertises context length as the primary differentiator, this bet fails.
ideas.signal: MemT-1.0, Kronecker Delta Rule, Competing Learning in Hybrid Architectures

ideas.title: Prediction: Physical RSI will be demonstrated in a *single* embodied system within 24 months, but it will be narrow — the system will improve at one task family, not general manipulation.
ideas.body: The scaling law work [Where is Physical RSI capability from?] and HarnessPro's recursive self-improvement [HarnessPro] suggest the pieces are in place. The contrarian bet is that RSI shows up in *narrow* physical domains first (e.g., a robot that gets better at assembly through self-practice), not as general capability. Falsifiable: if no single-system physical RSI is demonstrated by late 2028, the bet fails.
ideas.signal: Where is Physical RSI capability from?, HarnessPro

ideas.title: Prediction: The "open weights are back" narrative [Interconnects] is a local maximum — within 12 months, a major open-weight release will be *withdrawn or neutered* due to a security incident, and the open/closed debate will shift from ideology to liability.
ideas.body: The OpenCode hack [TechCrunch AI] and Meta's scraping terms reversal [TechCrunch AI] show the fragility of open ecosystems. The contrarian bet: a serious incident (not just API key theft, but a model-level exploit) forces a reckoning. Falsifiable: if no major open-weight model is withdrawn or restricted by late 2027, the bet fails.
ideas.signal: Interconnects on Meta, TechCrunch on OpenCode, The Verge on Meta scraping

ideas.title: Prediction: "Faithful adaptation" will become the dominant creative AI use case, displacing "generate from scratch" — and the winning products will be judged on *fidelity to source*, not visual quality.
ideas.body: Manga2Animate [Manga2Animate] and the broader trend toward agentic, reference-conditioned generation [RefCraft] suggest a shift from "make something new" to "adapt something existing." The contrarian bet: creative professionals will pay more for tools that *respect* their source material than for tools that generate novel content. Falsifiable: if the top-grossing creative AI tools in 2027 are still primarily "generate from prompt" rather than "adapt from source," the bet fails.
ideas.signal: Manga2Animate, RefCraft, Mise-en-Video

ideas.title: Prediction: The "AI slop" problem on Spotify [The Verge] is a preview of a broader *content provenance crisis* — and within 18 months, a major platform will be forced to *retroactively remove* AI-generated content that was initially accepted.
ideas.body: Spotify removed 50 million AI slop tracks [The Verge AI]. Falsifiable: if no major platform faces a public scandal over retroactive AI content removal by mid-2028, the bet fails.
ideas.signal: The Verge on Spotify, Google DeepMind on content provenance

ideas.title: Prediction: "Embedded evaluators" will fail as a governance mechanism — not because they're captured, but because they can't keep up with the *speed* of model iteration.
ideas.body: Hugging Face's policy chief is already skeptical of embedded evaluators [TechCrunch AI]. The contrarian bet: the evaluation bottleneck is not access or neutrality, but *latency* — by the time an evaluator certifies a model, it's already been superseded. Falsifiable: if embedded evaluators become a standard, effective part of frontier lab governance by 2028, the bet fails.
ideas.signal: TechCrunch on embedded evaluators, Quanta on Hardt

ideas.body: Figma's co-founder says MCP isn't perfect [TechCrunch AI], and websites are already blocking agents [The Verge AI]. The contrarian bet: the resolution is not a technical standard but a market — websites sell structured access to agents, and agents bid for it. Falsifiable: if MCP or a similar protocol becomes the dominant agent-access mechanism by 2028, the bet fails.
